**Adding condition effect on alpha:**
_running "grabowska_ez_fit_krakow_new.R" with "grabowska_ez_model_new" with with max tree depth and adapt delta on standard values_
Question: do the mean results come closer to the original ones when we add the condition effect on alpha

- NOTE: my paper resp = +1 = post-correct, resp = -1 = post-error, grabowska codes error= 1, correct= -1, other way round!
- answer: no, for alpha even slightly further off
- alpha intercept: in paper 1.48, for me 0.69 (half, as before)
- new: alpha condition: 0.45, for me 0.057 
- alpha resp_type: −0.09, for me 0.024 (sign flip is expected), as before 
- nu intercept: 4.03, for me 3.14, still 1 lower, as before
- nu condition: 3.07, for me 2.09, same 
- nu resp_type: −0.18, for me 0.128 (sign flip again expected), as before almost same
- interaction effect: 0.21, for me 0.41, again double the value, as before
- my model only has condition, response_type, and  interaction as predictors but the paper's model (Table 1) has a third predictor --> the ERN/CRN peak amplitude from the preceding trial (e_i) and its interactions
- my  coefficients are absorbing the variance that in the paper is explained by the EEG amplitude --> not estimating the same quantity


*new plots results*

- Resp_type slope on nu and Resp_type slope on alpha have wide individual credible intervals and many are crossing zero
- same as what the paper mentions as a limitation --> few error trials per person which inflates individual-level uncertainty --> hard to tell yet at the individual level whether there are differences
- alpha and nu both have the biggest visual separation in congruent vs. incongruent
- nu violins show interaction : post-error nu is way lower in congruent trials but stays about the same or slightly higher in incongruent trials 
- tau varies but is not modelled, maybe we should look at it too

**forest plot of the sigmas (random effects)**

- has all between person SDs: sigma_nu, sigma_alpha, sigma_tau --> residual (within-cell) SDs & sigma_nu_cond, sigma_nu_resp, sigma_nu_cr, sigma_alpha_resp --> between-person SDs of the random slopes
- sigma_nu_cond = 0.57 --> largest slope SD --> people vary a lot in how strongly congruency affects their drift rate
- sigma_nu_resp, sigma_nu_cr, sigma_alpha_resp a lot smaller & closer to zero --> some individual variability
- sigma_alpha is in the paper 0.26, and mine is way smaller, 0.072
- sigma_drift is kinda similar: 1.13 and 1.026 for mine 
- paper does not give a sigma_tau value


*Disclaimer*: I realized that the paper does it differently than us so now I made a new model with intercepts for nu, alpha, and tau that are person-specific random intercepts (nu_0[i], alpha_0[i], tau_0[i]) because we didn't have that. Instead we had single fixed population values (beta_nu[1], beta_alpha[1], beta_tau). The change now should make sigma_nu0/sigma_alpha0/sigma_tau0 more comparable to the paper's "intercept variability sigma" (Table 3) because sigma_nu/sigma_alpha/sigma_tau were conflated with between-person intercept differences. But then I realized that it only matters for tau since nu[i,k] is completely unconstrained (matrix[I,K] nu;) anyway, there are no boundaries. alpha[i,k] is bounded (matrix<lower=0.1, upper=3.0>[I,K] alpha;) but without T[] in sampling, so Stan constraints the parameter with the bounds, doesn't matter whether mu_alpha_ik (alpha_0[i]) is in the right bounds. An extreme alpha_0[i] would be a weird asymmetric prior and not an error. tau[i,k] is bounded and truncated (T[0.05,]) so only here the situation can be critical because tau_0[i] (mean of truncation) could theoretically be below 0.05 or negative, which would lead to numerical difficulties in fast trials (lots of mass at boundaries / truncation ends). The files for creation of this try out but now disregarded model are called _randint.stan_ and _randint.R_. 

It is good for comparison the per person parameters though, because their model has random intercepts. 


**Comparison per person --> learnings**

***Model without random intercepts (main model: grabowska_ez_model_new.stan / grabowska_ez_fit_krakow_new.R)***

- Only nu_c[i] (condition slope on drift rate) has a real person-specific counterpart in Grabowska's model (participants_delta_cond), as response-type and its interactions are fixed in their mode
- This comparison has an r = 0.85 but the parameter values lie about 1 point above theirs, similar to the population-level from before (b_nu_condition: 2.09 vs. 3.07) --> the difference seems to be a shift and maybe is because we are missing the EEG predictor
- Our model has no person-specific intercept for nu/alpha/tau (only beta_nu[1]/beta_alpha[1]/beta_tau, so shared), so we can only get a per-person "baseline" with a proxy: I did rowMeans() of the free parameters per cell (nu[i,k], alpha[i,k], tau[i,k]) across the 4 cells 
- this nu proxy versus the participants_delta got r = 0.90, which was surprisingly high, I am not sure if I did something stupid or if that means that we can still find the individual signal in cell-level EZ fits without the random intercept term
- the tau proxy versus participants_ter had r = 0.47, the alpha proxy versus participants_alpha had r = 0.21 (that looks like just noise)

***Model with random intercepts (grabowska_ez_model_randint.stan / grabowska_ez_fit_krakow_randint.R)***

- Adding nu_0[i]/alpha_0[i]/tau_0[i] gives us actual hierarchical intercepts so structurally it is then matching Grabowska's participants_delta/participants_alpha/participants_ter
- results: nu_0, r = 0.92; tau_0, r = 0.54 (slight improvement); alpha_0, r = 0.26 (only small improvement, still weak)
- nu_c is still at r = 0.85, it's the same parameter in both models
- alpha result not improving much --> sigma_alpha and sigma_alpha0 are weakly identified from each other in this model (Rhat up to 1.20 for sigma_alpha)
- the model can't reliably separate residual from intercept variance for alpha, so the individual alpha_0[i] estimates that it produces aren't precise enough to correlate strongly with an external benchmark 

--> Adriana: do we draw the same conclusions? 


**I ran a stability check with 3 runs to check whether there is a trade off**
***see: stability check plots and files auf GIt***

- mu_nu: 3.144, 3.142, 3.138
- mu_alpha: 0.6917, 0.6916, 0.6913
- b_nu_condition: 2.084, 2.090, 2.086
- sigma_nu: 1.024, 1.026, 1.023
- highest instability ratio: 1.97 (sigma_alpha_resp) but still not high
- highest Rhat across all parameters and all runs: 1.02 
- seems like the population-level estimates from this model are reproducible


**okay but why are they different than the paper??**

- option 1: we do not have the EEG predictor
- model includes the trial-level EEG amplitude (pre_ne_FCz_standardized) as a predictor and its interaction with response type
- EEG amplitude is correlated with response type 
- we dropped a predictor that was correlated with the ones we kept --> maybe our coefficients absorb the missing predictor's explained variance
- that could be why b_nu_condition too low, b_nu_interaction too high and mu_alpha about half the value
- option 2: the paper only has condition, EEG-amplitude, and EEG interaction with response-type varying by person, response_type is fixed, we let response_type vary by person
- option 3: condition effect on alpha is person-specific (participants_alpha_cond) in the paper, in my model its fixed --> bias the fixed estimate so there is more shrinkage??
- our b_alpha_condition (0.057) is a lot smaller so maybe thats why
